### I. The Weight of the Small Hours

There is a precise and unheralded hour—somewhere between three and four in the morning—when the architecture of the day completely collapses, and the architecture of the mind is forced to take its place. By then, the residual momentum of the evening has evaporated. The late-night traffic, which for hours maintains a thin, oceanic hiss against the edges of a city, thins to an occasional, haunting solitary engine: a taxi cutting through an intersection with the indifferent speed of a ghost, or a municipal sweeper scrubbing curbs that no one is awake to walk upon. 

If you are sitting awake at a desk during this hour, the world ceases to be an arena of action and becomes instead an archive of vibrations. The refrigerator in the kitchen resumes its low, mechanical grief, shuddering to life with a dry metallic rattle before settling into an icy drone. A radiator knocks once, twice, three times, like an impatient traveler at a locked hostel gate, then falls mute. The walls, which during noon are merely borders separating functional spaces—the room where one eats, the corridor where one walks, the threshold where one greets—revert to what they actually are: heavy, porous slabs of gypsum, lath, and dried pine, settling infinitesimally deeper into the subterranean mud, groaning under the simple, ancient burden of their own mass.

To be awake then is to occupy a strange, unauthorized clearing in human time. Modern life is organized entirely around the fiction that time is an isotropic medium—that an hour at ten o'clock in the morning possesses the exact same value, density, and moral character as an hour at three o'clock at night. The clock face, with its serene circular symmetry, insists upon this lie. It tells us that sixty minutes is sixty minutes, whether the sun is beating down upon the asphalt or whether the hemisphere has tilted into the shadow of its own body. 

Yet everyone who has ever stared into the ceiling at three in the morning knows that nocturnal time has a completely different viscosity. It does not flow; it pools. It gathers in corners like dust. Thoughts that would be laughed out of court at midday—petty humiliations from twenty years ago, sudden terrifying illuminations regarding the fragility of the carotid artery, bizarre linguistic loops where a single mundane word like *chimney* or *apricot* sheds its meaning and becomes an alien incantation—expand to fill the entire skull. The diurnal mind is an editor, swift, ruthless, and practical, cutting out the irrelevancies so that the body may navigate traffic, answer correspondence, and feed itself. The nocturnal mind is an archivist driven slightly mad by isolation, pulling forgotten files from dusty cabinets and spreading them across the floor with manic, trembling fingers.

We speak often of silence, but what we encounter in the deep night is not the absence of sound; it is the radical lowering of the noise floor. When the grand orchestra of collective human utility falls quiet, the world begins to whisper its private secrets. You hear the paper fibers of an open book drying out in the winter air; you hear the ticking of a wrist-watch resting on a bedside table four feet away, a tiny, relentless guillotine severing the seconds from the future and dropping them into the past; you hear, if you sit still enough, the high, thin, electrical singing of your own nervous system, that interior telephone exchange carrying messages from nowhere to nowhere.

---

### II. The Extinction of the Dark

Human beings have spent the last three centuries waging a sustained, triumphant, and catastrophic war against the dark. It is easy to understand why. For almost the entirety of our species’ history, nightfall was not a mood; it was an iron wall. It meant freezing cold, predatory threat, immobility, and the terrible contraction of human agency to the radius of a smoky resin torch or a tallow candle that smelled of boiled mutton. In the medieval European city, the closing of the city gates at sundown was an absolute division: inside, a shuttered, suspicious huddle; outside, the wild domain of footpads, wolves, and the supernatural horrors that populated the unlit countryside.

The invention of artificial illumination was therefore greeted as the greatest of human salvations. When the first gas lamps were ignited along the Pall Mall in London in the early nineteenth century, observers did not merely remark upon the visibility; they spoke in religious tones of the banishment of evil, the triumph of reason, and the dawn of a perpetual day. With gas, and then with the incandescent bulb, humanity broke the oldest curfew in the world. We seized the night and forced it to labor for us. We built night shifts, twenty-four-hour factories, illuminated shop windows that sold goods to sleepwalkers, and highways that cut through the countryside like blazing ribbons of industrial optimism.

Yet in banishing the dark, we have inadvertently severed our connection to one of our most essential cognitive landscapes. Darkness was once the great solvent of human hubris. To walk out into a medieval or ancient night was to be immediately crushed by the sheer, terrifying majesty of the cosmos. The Milky Way was not an abstraction glimpsed in long-exposure photographs taken by orbital telescopes; it was a luminous, curdled river of silver spanning from horizon to horizon, so bright that on clear nights it could cast faint, ethereal shadows on a whitewashed wall. The stars were not decorative pinpricks; they were the terrifyingly real ceiling of the human dwelling, an undeniable proof that our small fires were insignificant specks in an infinite, cold abyss.

This sight instilled an involuntary modesty. It was impossible to look up into that sprawling vault night after night and believe that one’s local grievances, political factions, or mercantile balance sheets were the axis upon which the universe turned. The night demanded contemplation; it demanded that the individual confront the terrifying reality of their own finitude.

Today, eight out of ten children born in North America and Europe will never see the Milky Way with their own eyes. They grow up beneath an amber dome of light pollution, a luminous smog created by poorly aimed streetlamps, sports stadiums, parking lots, and digital billboards. Our sky has been painted over with a dull, yellowish-gray wash. We have traded the infinite horizon for a low, artificial ceiling. We live inside a brightly lit terrarium of our own making, and as a consequence, our interior lives have become correspondingly shallow. 

When we extinguished the dark outside, we also began to extinguish the dark inside ourselves. We have developed an almost pathological terror of the unilluminated space. We take our glowing rectangles to bed with us; we bathe our retinas in the cold, blue phosphor of screens until the very moment our eyelids falter. We scroll through frantic dispatches from distant continents, through trivial arguments conducted by strangers, through algorithmic streams of images designed specifically to ensure that the mind is never left alone with itself. We do this because the moment the screen goes black, the vast, unlit silence of the room rushes in, and with it comes that ancient, uncomfortable question that the dark has always asked of us: *Who are you when you are not performing?*

---

### III. The Glosa and the Palimpsest

In the abbey library of St. Gall in Switzerland, there are manuscripts dating from the eighth and ninth centuries that bear in their margins the tiny, scratched testimonies of the men who copied them. These monks were not machines; they were flesh and blood, shivering in scriptoria where fires were forbidden for fear of incinerating the parchment. As they copied the Latin homilies of Augustine or the intricate logic of Boethius, their attention would inevitably waver. The eye would wander from the exemplar to the narrow strip of bare vellum at the edge of the leaf, and there, using the very quill and iron-gall ink meant for the sacred text, they would write down their misery.

*"O, my hand,"* one scribe writes in Old Irish at the margin of a copy of Cassiodorus. 
Another notes simply: *"The ink is thin; the parchment is hairy."* 
A third, evidently freezing to death over his desk in the dead of winter, scrawls: *"It is cold today; it is natural; it is winter."* 
And perhaps the most heartbreakingly human of them all: *"Now I have written the whole thing; for Christ’s sake give me a drink."*

These marginalia—the *glosa*—are often far more moving to the modern reader than the main texts they frame. The main text is an monument; the margin is a breath. The main text represents the official culture, the theological consensus, the desperate human effort to construct an eternal, immutable truth out of words. But the margin is the record of the shivering hand that held the pen, the toothache that would not subside, the candle that was guttering in the draft, the stray cat that walked across the drying wet ink (leaving permanent paw prints that still survive in archives from Dubrovnik to Hereford).

There is a profound comfort in these errors and intrusions. They remind us that culture is not an immaculate edifice handed down from heaven, but a fragile, improvised shelter assembled by cold, hungry, distracted people who were constantly on the verge of falling asleep. 

Consider the palimpsest: a piece of parchment that, because of the scarcity and expense of animal skins, was scraped clean with pumice stone so that a new text could be written over the old one. In the nineteenth century, scholars discovered that by using chemical reagents (and later, ultraviolet photography and multi-spectral imaging), they could read the faint, ghostly traces of the under-text that had been scrubbed away centuries prior. Beneath a dry, pedestrian fourteenth-century book of prayers, one might suddenly find the long-lost verses of Euripides, or a forgotten treatise on geometry by Archimedes, or the passionate legal arguments of Cicero.

We are all, in our own ways, living palimpsests. No one ever arrives at maturity with a clean slate. Every experience we undergo, every conversation we endure, every landscape we pass through is inscribed upon the nervous system. We try to scrub them away. We undergo therapies; we change cities; we alter our habits; we declare ourselves "reinvented." We write new identities across the surface of our lives in bold, assertive, modern scripts—careers, marriages, philosophies, aesthetic tastes. 

Yet underneath, if the light hits the page at just the right angle, the old text remains legible. The childhood terror of the dark hallway; the scent of rain on dry bitumen in a town we haven't visited in thirty years; the specific cadence of a mother’s voice calling from a back porch on an August evening that ended before the fall of the Berlin Wall—none of it is ever truly erased. It is merely overwritten. In the quiet hours of the night, when the top layer of ink has dried and the mind’s defenses are down, the under-text bleeds through. We find ourselves reading the old, forgotten script, surprised to discover that the person we were at twelve years old is still sitting down there in the dark, waiting for the ink to dry.

---

### IV. Nocturnes of Steel and Water

There is a distinct genre of melancholy that belongs exclusively to the modern infrastructural world late at night. 

If you drive three hours out of any major metropolis at midnight, heading into the agricultural or post-industrial hinterlands, you will encounter a landscape that daylight renders utterly banal, but which darkness transfigures into something mythic and monumental. You see the vast logistical distribution centers—those windowless, corrugated-steel cathedrals of consumption, each covering twenty or thirty acres of leveled ground, surrounded by moats of yellow asphalt upon which hundreds of shipping containers sit like the sarcophagi of forgotten giants. 

These facilities never sleep. Their interior illumination is clinical, shadowless, and invariant—a blinding, eternal high noon designed to ensure that the barcode scanners never miss a register and the forklift operators never drift into reverie. From the highway, they look like landed spaceships, humongous terrestrial organisms that have settled onto the cornfields to ingest and excrete the physical matter of modern life: plastic toys manufactured in Shenzhen, frozen pork bellies from Iowa, cheap cotton shirts stitched in Bangladesh, flat-screen monitors, boxes of ibuprofen, microfibers, motor oil.

Nearby, the high-voltage transmission towers march across the hills. By day, they are clumsy steel skeletons, an eyesore against the treeline. But at night, they become magnificent and ominous. If you stand directly beneath one of them in the damp air after a rainstorm, you can hear the electricity coursing through the cables: a dry, venomous, bacon-fat sizzle, the sound of five hundred thousand volts hanging suspended fifty feet above your skull. It is the raw, unmediated circulatory system of our civilization, pumping energy from remote coal plants, nuclear reactors, and wind farms into the sleeping bedrooms of millions of people who will awake tomorrow morning and press the button on an electric kettle without ever considering the vast, vibrating web of steel and aluminum that made their water boil.

And then there are the water treatment plants, the sewage plants, the data centers. Especially the data centers: those monolithic, bunker-like buildings nestled near rural fiber-optic trunk lines, protected by barbed wire and security cameras, their only external sign of life the massive, deafening banks of chiller fans roaring in the dark. Inside those concrete vaults, millions of tiny silicon wafers are baking in racks, their copper circuits glowing with the digital ghosts of humanity: billions of hours of streaming video, trillions of search queries, old bank balances, photos of vacations taken by dead people, love letters sent via encrypted messaging apps, algorithms predicting the price of wheat in Chicago three weeks from now. 

To stand outside a data center at three in the morning is to realize that our collective memory no longer resides in the human brain, nor in the tactile leaves of books, but in these roaring, air-conditioned warehouses in the middle of nowhere. If the power were to cut out, if the diesel backup generators failed to cough to life, an entire civilization's culture, history, and personal archives would not burn like the Library of Alexandria—they would simply cease to exist, dissolving into the ether without leaving behind so much as a pinch of ash or the smell of smoke.

---

### V. The Mirage of Total Recall

We live under the reign of an unprecedented fantasy: the fantasy of the total archive. Never before has a culture believed that it could—and should—save everything. Every photograph taken on an iPhone is uploaded to a server farm; every text message, every credit card transaction, every pedestrian step recorded by an accelerometer is indexed, cataloged, and preserved. We have built an electronic panopticon, not only to watch ourselves, but to prevent ourselves from ever losing a single crumb of our passage through the world.

Yet this mania for preservation is fundamentally anti-human. The human mind was never designed to remember everything. Biological memory is an engine of triage; it is an artist that paints using omission as its primary technique. 

In Jorge Luis Borges’ famous short story, "Funes the Memorious," a young Uruguayan man falls from a horse and awakens to find that his perception and memory have become absolute. He remembers the shapes of the clouds in the southern sky on the dawn of the thirtieth of April, 1882, and can compare them in his memory to the streaks on the marbled binding of a book he saw only once in his childhood. He remembers every leaf on every tree he has ever passed, every foam-bubble on an oar stroke, every tooth in the comb of a dead horse.

At first, this seems like a godlike gift. But Borges quickly reveals the horror of Ireneo Funes’ condition: he cannot think. For to think, Borges writes, is to ignore differences; it is to generalize, to abstract, to simplify. In the crowded world of Funes, there was nothing but details, immediate and contiguous. He could not look at a dog from the side at three-fourteen in the afternoon and believe it was the same dog that had been seen from the front at three-fifteen. His mind was not an instrument of intelligence; it was a garbage heap of infinitely precise, infinitely useless data. He died young, Borges tells us, of congestion of the lungs—or perhaps, we suspect, choked to death by the sheer, unyielding volume of his own recall.

Our culture is rapidly becoming Funes. We are drowning in the granularity of our own documentation. We have so many photographs of our children that we no longer look at them; we have recorded so many hours of concerts, weddings, sunsets, and dinners that we have outsourced the actual experience of them to the lens. By attempting to save everything, we have devalued the act of attention.

Forgetting is not a flaw in our cognitive machinery; it is the very condition of our survival. Forgetting is the leaf-mold that falls upon the forest floor of the mind, rotting down the specific, sharp edges of the past so that new ideas, new metaphors, and new attachments can take root. Without forgetting, there can be no forgiveness, for forgiveness requires that the acute sting of an injury be allowed to blur into the soft, indeterminate wash of time. Without forgetting, there can be no poetry, for poetry relies upon the imperfect, longing recollection of things that are absent, not the cold, HD replay of things that are mechanically preserved.

When an ancient Greek died, they believed their soul was led to the Underworld, where two rivers flowed: Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, and Mnemosyne, the river of memory. The initiates of the Orphic mysteries were instructed to avoid Lethe and drink only from Mnemosyne, so that their souls would remember their divine origins. But the ordinary dead drank deeply from Lethe, washing away the specific, agonizing griefs and joys of their mortal lives so that they might be born again without the crushing weight of their previous incarnations. We have entirely damned up the river Lethe. We have built concrete levees along its banks and installed water pumps to drain it dry. We have forced ourselves to drink only from the cold, brackish waters of Mnemosyne, and we wonder why our society is so exhausted, so vengeful, so incapable of moving forward, so thoroughly poisoned by the unforgotten grudges of the past.

---

### VI. The Persistence of the Horizon

And yet, despite the noise, despite the light pollution, despite the mechanical roars of the servers and the relentless churn of the electronic archive, the physical world retains its stubborn, unbribable reality.

Eventually, the small hours must yield. It does not happen suddenly, but through an almost imperceptible redistribution of values. The ink-black tone of the window pane begins to soften, shifting first into a deep, bruised indigo, then into a slate-gray that has the cool, smooth texture of wet slate. 

Outside, the birds begin their rehearsals. It is not the exuberant, chaotic symphonic burst of mid-spring, but the tentative, sleepy chirps of the few who are testing the atmosphere. A single sparrow speaks from the rain gutter; a long pause follows, lasting several minutes, as if the bird were waiting for an answer from the other side of the world. Then, from two streets away, a robin replies. The social contract of the day is quietly being drafted again.

There is a immense, cleansing dignity in this transition. The night, with all its private terrors, its excessive nostalgias, its terrifying clarity, begins to fold up its tents. The things in the room—the chair, the coat hanging over the back of the door, the cold cup of tea, the books stacked haphazardly on the floor—step out of the shadows and reclaim their daylight identities. They stop being symbols of existential dread and return to being furniture.

This is the great, unearned mercy of being alive on this planet: the world resets itself. No matter how thoroughly you have ruined your life in the small hours of your mind, no matter how profoundly you have convinced yourself of the ultimate vanity of all human endeavor, the dawn arrives with total indifference to your despair. It does not ask for your permission; it does not demand that you have solved the riddle of your existence before it casts its first, cool light across the chimney pots.

To step outside onto the porch at this hour is to receive an unexpected gift. The air smells entirely different than it did at dusk; it has been scrubbed clean by the night's descent, carrying the sharp, vegetal scent of dew condensing on cold grass, the earthy odor of soil, the faint hint of woodsmoke from a chimney two miles away. The asphalt is damp. The sky in the east is no longer slate, but an astonishing, tender lemon-yellow, cut through with long, horizontal striations of peach-colored cloud.

For a few fleeting minutes, before the alarms begin to chime on nightstands, before the school buses begin their yellow patrols, before the emails begin to drop into inboxes with their small, insistent pings of urgency, the world is clean. It belongs to no one. It has no market value; it cannot be monetized, cataloged, or searched. It is simply there: massive, physical, ancient, and entirely indifferent to the species that scurries across its crust.

You breathe in that cool, unowned air, and you feel the small, miraculous machinery of your lungs expand and contract. You are tired down to the very marrow of your bones; your eyes are dry and hot from lack of sleep; your thoughts are scattered like dead leaves. But you are here. The night did not swallow you, as it sometimes threatened to do. The sun, that blind, roaring ball of hydrogen four hundred times the size of the moon, has cleared the edge of the planet once again. 

You turn back inside, shut the door against the morning chill, turn off the desk lamp that has burned uselessly into the daylight, and finally, gratefully, lay your head down upon the pillow. The light spills across the floor, tracing the old, familiar grain of the wood, quiet, patient, and infinite, waiting for you to wake.

Inside those concrete vaults, millions of tiny silicon wafers are baking in racks, their copper circuits glowing with the digital ghosts of humanity: billions of hours of streaming video, trillions of search queries, old bank balances, photos of vacations taken by dead people, love letters sent via encrypted messaging apps, algorithms predicting the price of wheat in Chicago three weeks from now. 

To stand outside a data center at three in the morning is to realize that our collective memory no longer resides in the human brain, nor in the tactile leaves of books, but in these roaring, air-conditioned warehouses in the middle of nowhere. If the power were to cut out, if the diesel backup generators failed to cough to life, an entire civilization's culture, history, and personal archives would not burn like the Library of Alexandria—they would simply cease to exist, dissolving into the ether without leaving behind so much as a pinch of ash or the smell of smoke.

---

### V. The Mirage of Total Recall

We live under the reign of an unprecedented fantasy: the fantasy of the total archive. Never before has a culture believed that it could—and should—save everything. Every photograph taken on an iPhone is uploaded to a server farm; every text message, every credit card transaction, every pedestrian step recorded by an accelerometer is indexed, cataloged, and preserved. We have built an electronic panopticon, not only to watch ourselves, but to prevent ourselves from ever losing a single crumb of our passage through the world.

Yet this mania for preservation is fundamentally anti-human. The human mind was never designed to remember everything. Biological memory is an engine of triage; it is an artist that paints using omission as its primary technique. 

In Jorge Luis Borges’ famous short story, "Funes the Memorious," a young Uruguayan man falls from a horse and awakens to find that his perception and memory have become absolute. He remembers the shapes of the clouds in the southern sky on the dawn of the thirtieth of April, 1882, and can compare them in his memory to the streaks on the marbled binding of a book he saw only once in his childhood. He remembers every leaf on every tree he has ever passed, every foam-bubble on an oar stroke, every tooth in the comb of a dead horse.

At first, this seems like a godlike gift. But Borges quickly reveals the horror of Ireneo Funes’ condition: he cannot think. For to think, Borges writes, is to ignore differences; it is to generalize, to abstract, to simplify. In the crowded world of Funes, there was nothing but details, immediate and contiguous. He could not look at a dog from the side at three-fourteen in the afternoon and believe it was the same dog that had been seen from the front at three-fifteen. His mind was not an instrument of intelligence; it was a garbage heap of infinitely precise, infinitely useless data. He died young, Borges tells us, of congestion of the lungs—or perhaps, we suspect, choked to death by the sheer, unyielding volume of his own recall.

Our culture is rapidly becoming Funes. We are drowning in the granularity of our own documentation. We have so many photographs of our children that we no longer look at them; we have recorded so many hours of concerts, weddings, sunsets, and dinners that we have outsourced the actual experience of them to the lens. By attempting to save everything, we have devalued the act of attention.

Forgetting is not a flaw in our cognitive machinery; it is the very condition of our survival. Forgetting is the leaf-mold that falls upon the forest floor of the mind, rotting down the specific, sharp edges of the past so that new ideas, new metaphors, and new attachments can take root. Without forgetting, there can be no forgiveness, for forgiveness requires that the acute sting of an injury be allowed to blur into the soft, indeterminate wash of time. Without forgetting, there can be no poetry, for poetry relies upon the imperfect, longing recollection of things that are absent, not the cold, HD replay of things that are mechanically preserved.

When an ancient Greek died, they believed their soul was led to the Underworld, where two rivers flowed: Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, and Mnemosyne, the river of memory. The initiates of the Orphic mysteries were instructed to avoid Lethe and drink only from Mnemosyne, so that their souls would remember their divine origins. But the ordinary dead drank deeply from Lethe, washing away the specific, agonizing griefs and joys of their mortal lives so that they might be born again without the crushing weight of their previous incarnations. We have entirely damned up the river Lethe. We have built concrete levees along its banks and installed water pumps to drain it dry. We have forced ourselves to drink only from the cold, brackish waters of Mnemosyne, and we wonder why our society is so exhausted, so vengeful, so incapable of moving forward, so thoroughly poisoned by the unforgotten grudges of the past.

---

### VI. The Persistence of the Horizon

And yet, despite the noise, despite the light pollution, despite the mechanical roars of the servers and the relentless churn of the electronic archive, the physical world retains its stubborn, unbribable reality.

Eventually, the small hours must yield. It does not happen suddenly, but through an almost imperceptible redistribution of values. The ink-black tone of the window pane begins to soften, shifting first into a deep, bruised indigo, then into a slate-gray that has the cool, smooth texture of wet slate. 

Outside, the birds begin their rehearsals. It is not the exuberant, chaotic symphonic burst of mid-spring, but the tentative, sleepy chirps of the few who are testing the atmosphere. A single sparrow speaks from the rain gutter; a long pause follows, lasting several minutes, as if the bird were waiting for an answer from the other side of the world. Then, from two streets away, a robin replies. The social contract of the day is quietly being drafted again.

There is a immense, cleansing dignity in this transition. The night, with all its private terrors, its excessive nostalgias, its terrifying clarity, begins to fold up its tents. The things in the room—the chair, the coat hanging over the back of the door, the cold cup of tea, the books stacked haphazardly on the floor—step out of the shadows and reclaim their daylight identities. They stop being symbols of existential dread and return to being furniture.

This is the great, unearned mercy of being alive on this planet: the world resets itself. No matter how thoroughly you have ruined your life in the small hours of your mind, no matter how profoundly you have convinced yourself of the ultimate vanity of all human endeavor, the dawn arrives with total indifference to your despair. It does not ask for your permission; it does not demand that you have solved the riddle of your existence before it casts its first, cool light across the chimney pots.

To step outside onto the porch at this hour is to receive an unexpected gift. The air smells entirely different than it did at dusk; it has been scrubbed clean by the night's descent, carrying the sharp, vegetal scent of dew condensing on cold grass, the earthy odor of soil, the faint hint of woodsmoke from a chimney two miles away. The asphalt is damp. The sky in the east is no longer slate, but an astonishing, tender lemon-yellow, cut through with long, horizontal striations of peach-colored cloud.

For a few fleeting minutes, before the alarms begin to chime on nightstands, before the school buses begin their yellow patrols, before the emails begin to drop into inboxes with their small, insistent pings of urgency, the world is clean. It belongs to no one. It has no market value; it cannot be monetized, cataloged, or searched. It is simply there: massive, physical, ancient, and entirely indifferent to the species that scurries across its crust.

You breathe in that cool, unowned air, and you feel the small, miraculous machinery of your lungs expand and contract. You are tired down to the very marrow of your bones; your eyes are dry and hot from lack of sleep; your thoughts are scattered like dead leaves. But you are here. The night did not swallow you, as it sometimes threatened to do. The sun, that blind, roaring ball of hydrogen four hundred times the size of the moon, has cleared the edge of the planet once again. 

You turn back inside, shut the door against the morning chill, turn off the desk lamp that has burned uselessly into the daylight, and finally, gratefully, lay your head down upon the pillow. The light spills across the floor, tracing the old, familiar grain of the wood, quiet, patient, and infinite, waiting for you to wake.
